title: Verifiable blind quantum computing: Comparative analysis and design considerations for client architectures
authors: Janice van Dam, Jeroen Grimbergen, Stephanie D. C. Wehner
abstract: Blind quantum computing (BQC) allows a client to delegate quantum computations to a remote server without revealing the input, computation, or output. In addition to being blind, the client can sometimes also verify that the server has performed their instructions correctly, a property known as verifiability. A key part of realizing such verifiable BQC (VBQC) is choosing the design of the client device: many architectures have been proposed, each with different hardware requirements, security properties, and performance characteristics, making it difficult to identify which is most suitable for a given implementation. In this work, we present a comparative analysis of client architectures for VBQC with a matter-qubit server. We restrict our analysis to single-server, single-client protocols with information-theoretic security based on measurement-based quantum computation. We identify three main categories of client: emission-based, measurement-based, and rotation-based, each with multiple variants depending on how the client interacts with the server. We evaluate each across different dimensions: we compare guarantees of existing corresponding security proofs, we derive equations for the rate at which each client can execute a protocol, we provide an overview of each architecture's error behaviour, and discuss hardware cost and design considerations. Client architectures implementing measurement-based remote state preparation and reflection-based teleportation emerge as strong default candidates, but as the right choice remains context-dependent, we provide a framework for navigating considerations to guide the selection of the most suitable architecture for a given setting.
summary: This work conducts a comprehensive comparison of client device architectures designed for Verifiable Blind Quantum Computing (VBQC). By analyzing emission-based, measurement-based, and rotation-based approaches using photonic qubits against a matter-qubit server, it establishes a framework to guide the selection of the most suitable architecture based on specific security or performance requirements.
main_problem: The paper addresses Verifiable Blind Quantum Computing (VBQC), which allows a client to delegate quantum computations while ensuring privacy and verifying the server's correct execution.
main_result: It provides a comparative analysis of three main client architectures—emission-based, measurement-based, and rotation-based—for VBQC with a matter-qubit server.
method: The authors compare these architectures across security guarantees, derived rate equations, error behavior, and hardware cost using information-theoretic security models.
model_or_system: The analysis is restricted to single-server, single-client protocols based on measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC), utilizing photonic qubits for communication with a matter-qubit server.
key_observables: Security guarantees, protocol execution rates, error behavior, and hardware cost/design considerations.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of matter qubits for the server and photonic qubits for communication, focusing on single-user scenarios.
figures_summary: Figure 1 depicts a taxonomy classifying client architectures into emission-based, measurement-based, and rotation-based categories.
paper_structure: The paper systematically classifies client capabilities (Emission, Measurement, Rotation) by detailing the physical mechanisms for state transfer within each category, followed by a comparative evaluation across multiple performance dimensions.
why_interesting: It directly compares hardware implementations for quantum computation protocols, offering guidance on selecting optimal architectures based on practical constraints like error rates and required fidelity.
